```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

## Introduction

This tutorial estimates complexity of infection (COI) and multi-locus allele frequencies with SNP-Slice. The algorithm is from [Ju, Liu, and He (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btae344). Their [original repository](https://github.com/nianqiaoju/snp-slice) is a set of scripts rather than an R package, and those scripts are difficult to install and run.

The example uses [`snp.slicer`](https://github.com/plasmogenepi/snp.slicer), an R package that implements that algorithm. Install it with the [installation instructions](installation.Rmd) before running the code below.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(vcfR)
library(snp.slicer)
library(kableExtra)
```

## The data

The data are the simulated sanger 100-SNP barcode: 100 polyclonal infections, 50 drawn from Bangladesh and 50 from Ghana. The file is described with the other [SNP barcode data](../../website_docs/data_snps.qmd).

`snp_slice()` reads a data frame with one row per observed allele:

- `specimen_id`: sample name
- `target_id`: SNP name
- `target_value`: allele code
- `target_count`: read count for that allele

The VCF stores allelic depth in `FORMAT/AD`. The two numbers are the reference-allele count and the alternate-allele count. Those become `target_value` `"0"` and `"1"`.

```{r}
vcf_data <- read.vcfR(
  here::here("data/snp_barcode/SpotMalariapfPanel_simData_sanger100.vcf.gz")
)

counts_raw <- t(vcfR::extract.gt(vcf_data, element = "AD"))

read0 <- vcfR::masplit(
  counts_raw, record = 1, sort = FALSE, decreasing = FALSE
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "specimen_id") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -specimen_id,
    names_to = "target_id",
    values_to = "target_count"
  ) |>
  mutate(target_value = "0")

read1 <- vcfR::masplit(
  counts_raw, record = 2, sort = FALSE, decreasing = FALSE
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "specimen_id") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -specimen_id,
    names_to = "target_id",
    values_to = "target_count"
  ) |>
  mutate(target_value = "1")

snpslice_data <- rbind(read0, read1) |>
  arrange(specimen_id, target_id)

snpslice_data |>
  slice_head(n = 6) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

## Run SNP-Slice

`snp_slice()` fits the model by MCMC. The default keeps 10,000 samples after burn-in. This page uses `n_sample = 100` so the example finishes quickly. Read the summary it prints: a short chain often has not converged, and those estimates are only there to show the output. Use the default `n_sample` for an analysis you will interpret.

`model = "negative_binomial"` uses the read counts. `seed` makes this short run repeatable.

```{r}
run <- snp_slice(
  snpslice_data,
  model = "negative_binomial",
  n_sample = 100,
  seed = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)

summary(run)
```

## Multi-locus allele frequencies

`calculate_allele_frequencies()` treats a set of SNPs as one haplotype. Each row is one haplotype across the SNPs you name, in that order. In the allele string, `0` is the reference allele and `1` is the alternate allele. `frequency` is the proportion of inferred parasite strains that carry that haplotype, and the frequencies sum to 1.

The default estimate is the final sample of the chain. Set `estimate = "posterior"` and rerun `snp_slice()` with `store_mcmc = TRUE` when you want a credible interval. That needs a longer chain than the one above.

```{r}
allele_freqs <- calculate_allele_frequencies(
  run,
  c("Pf3D7_01_v3_145515", "Pf3D7_01_v3_179347", "Pf3D7_01_v3_180554")
)

allele_freqs |>
  kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

## Complexity of infection

`calculate_individual_coi()` returns one COI per specimen from that same final sample. The uncertainty columns are empty for a point estimate. They are filled when `estimate = "posterior"` and the MCMC samples were stored.

```{r}
coi <- calculate_individual_coi(run)

coi |>
  slice_head(n = 6) |>
  kable(digits = 2) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

```{r}
ggplot(coi, aes(x = coi_estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, color = "white", fill = "#325b74") +
  theme_linedraw() +
  labs(x = "COI", y = "Samples")
```

## Summary

`snp.slicer` runs the SNP-Slice algorithm of Ju, Liu, and He on a table of allele read counts. This example estimated COI for each simulated infection and the frequency of haplotypes across three barcode SNPs. Cite the [Bioinformatics paper](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btae344) for the method. The original scripts remain in [nianqiaoju/snp-slice](https://github.com/nianqiaoju/snp-slice).
